The inspection report landed the night before the shipment was supposed to leave the port in Ningbo.

I'd approved the sample three weeks earlier. Same mold, same material, same supplier I'd used twice before. This was supposed to be routine.

Then I saw the number: 4.2 percent of the 3,000-unit batch flagged for surface defects.

I called the factory. They didn't deny it. "That's within the standard tolerance for this product category." Fair enough, I thought — that's the industry benchmark.

Except when I pulled up our order confirmation to double check, there was no defect tolerance written anywhere in it. Not in the contract, not in the email thread, nowhere.

I asked them straight: if we never agreed on a number, whose two and a half percent were we even using?

They went quiet for a few hours. Then sent one line back: "This is the level we've always used with buyers who don't specify one."

I hadn't thought about it, because I didn't know I had to.

Rossell Techsys is one company that we can track closely next quarters

Lets talk about the company here from scratch

The company works mainly in two segments: 

Wiring harnesses (70% of revenues) which are used in aerospace & defence, semiconductors and space satellites which is supposedly higher margin segments

The rest 30% is basically three things beyond wiring harness: 

(A) Electrical panel assemblies, which is the metal box where the switches and safety devices sit, wired up and ready to bolt onto the aircraft. 
(B) Electronic systems and systems integration, which is circuit boards with the chips already placed (the PCBs).  (C) Automatic test equipment, the rigs that OEMs keep in their own factories to check whether an electronic unit works before it is cleared to fly.

That is the whole company in simple language

For fourteen years, from 2011 to 2025, Rossell delivered mostly to one customer (Boeing), one product, flat as a table. Boeing wire harnesses and not much else.

Then something broke open.

The customer count went from four to more than thirty. The same harness-making capability turned out to sell into semiconductor fab equipment and into satellites, where the volumes are far larger than defence ever was.

Revenue went ₹217 crore in FY24, ₹259 crore in FY25, then ₹485 crore in FY26. Boeing as a customer was 99% of revenue until 2023 and is now around 40%. 

The forward story from here has two legs.

One, diversification away from Boeing. The FY27 target is a 50-50 split between defence and non-defence, with semiconductor and space carrying the growth.

Two, moving up the value chain. From loose harnesses to panels to fully integrated electromechanical assemblies. They frame it as content per aircraft going from 2% today to 15% to eventually 25%. More revenue from the same platforms, at better margin.

Funding all of it is a ₹300 crore QIP earmarked for capacity, systems and working capital.

The top line growth supports this and there is no question that sales growth is strong here. They grew sales by 78% in Q1 FY27

Their order book was ₹715 crore at March 2026 and ₹800 crore by June. Strategic agreements of ₹3,000 crore sit above that. During FY26 they submitted bids worth ₹4,500 crore. Roughly half the confirmed order book is now non-aerospace, which actually supports the diversification claim

The story parts way in two parts

Margin has gone the wrong way while the mix supposedly improved

EBITDA margin was 14.8% in FY25, 13.7%  in FY26 and 15.1% in Q1 FY27. Material cost ran 62.5% of revenue in FY26, so gross margin sits around 37 to 38%. 

At the start of FY26 management guided to 17 to 18% EBITDA margin. They delivered 13.7%. Back in the August 2025 call they were talking about 18 to 22%  in the short term.

So they did miss out the margins. The explanation each time is the same. First article inspections, training, qualification costs on new programmes will take a hit on margins while it improves once these move into steady production.

That may well be true. But semiconductor and space are already roughly a quarter of revenue, and those are the exact segments described as higher margin. If mix were the lever management says it is, some of it should be visible by now. It isn't.

The bigger issue is that this growth eats cash instead of producing it

Rossell generated ₹61 crore of operating profit before working capital in FY26. Working capital then swallowed ₹136 crore of it. Inventory alone absorbed ₹97 crore, receivables another ₹44 crore. Net cash from operations came in at negative ₹81.6 crore, which is worse than the minus ₹42 crore of FY25.

That gap was filled almost entirely with bank borrowing. Net working capital loans drawn during FY26 came to ₹174 crore.

The bit that ties it all together

The ₹300 crore QIP is important here. To execute an ₹800 crore order book plus ₹3,000 crore of strategic agreements, working capital has to expand further, not shrink. 

The QIP was expected to close by December 2025. By February 2026 it had slipped and management declined to give a new timeline. In the Q1 FY27 presentation it is still described as proposed. That is roughly nine months of slippage on the single item the growth plan depends on.

Management frames the delay as waiting for the right investor. Possibly. It is also true that raising ₹300 crore against a ₹152 crore net worth is heavy dilution, and that a company posting negative operating cash flow has less leverage in that negotiation than one posting positive.

The demand story is supported. Growth is real, order-backed and diversifying away from a single customer. The tailwinds behind it are structural rather than cyclical. 

The financial story is not supported yet. Margins have missed guidance twice and have moved opposite to what the mix shift predicts. The business consumes more cash the faster it runs. 

The next two quarters are unusually informative here. Watch the QIP.  Watch whether gross margin turns up while semiconductor and space mix keeps rising, because that last one is the honest test of whether moving up the value chain is a strategy or just a slide.

Under GDPR, erasure happens when a user asks for it. Under the DPDP Rules, erasure also runs on a timer: Rule 8 requires covered platforms to erase a dormant user's data after three years, whether or not anyone asked, and section 8(7) of the Act requires erasure once the purpose is served.

A GDPR erasure programme handles requests as they arrive. A DPDP erasure programme also needs a scheduled process that finds dormant accounts and erases them on time across the whole user base. Rule 8 commences on 13 May 2027.

text:
India has quietly frozen Starlink. It issued the license nearly a year ago, then let the final security clearance sit, and the whole satellite-comms sector has slowed with it. This is not a compliance dispute. New Delhi is asking a question Starlink can't really answer: given its US ownership and global network, how can it promise to follow Indian rules when Washington wants the opposite?

What spooked them is concrete. Starlink terminals were used in the Iran war even though it holds no license in Iran. India watched a sovereign state fail to switch off a network running over its own territory, and asked who is next.

Notice the tell. Jio and Bharti get an easier ride because their satellite partners are European, not a US-controlled operator. The worry isn't the satellites, it's whose hand is on the switch. And it lands days before SpaceX's IPO at a $1.75tn valuation, with Starlink as the main revenue engine, a reminder that the global rollout is far from uniform: shut out of China, and now stuck in India too.

text:
Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

My sister's daughter is in boarding school. She was dropped off on Sunday morning by her parents. That same Sunday evening I saw someone that looked like her in a busy road holding hands with a guy. 

Before the Keke could drop me off, I didn't see them again. I was so worried, I called her mom to know if she's at home that was when her mom told me she was dropped in school that morning. She's in ss 2. 

When I drop the call, I decided to go to her school because I didn't tell her mom anything until I'm so sure so that I won't cause problems for myself. 

So I went to her school, it took me an hour to get to her school and it was almost 9 pm. When I got there I met with the gate man. I told him I want to get something from my niece that she is with my key and I can't go inside my house, all he has to do is to get the key for me. Without letting me inside the school premises or even bring her out. He told me to wait that he has to notify her house mistress. A tall woman came with a flashlight and saw me and I reminded her that I'm the one that always come to see her on their visiting day. She quickly recognized me and said okay, let her go and get the keys for me. I waited and when she came out she told me she couldn't find her, I waited again for her to searched everywhere she was still not found. That was when another house mistress said she saw her leaving the school gate in the afternoon and she said her dad told her to follow them so she could pick something from the supermarket, that she will be back immediately, she was signed out by the morning security. 

I then told her house mistress what I saw and her parents were called. Her dad said he never asked her to follow them. That they bought everything she would need till their next visit. 

My sister cried without sleeping throughout the night and she doesn't have a phone. 

By Monday morning she was in school. Her mom got her arrested and demand to know where the guy she spent the night lives, she took the police there. A university guy in his second year. On our way she was crying and begging the police not to arrest the guy. Her dad had already told the police he wants the guy arrested. 

My niece said if they arrest the guy they should arrest her also. My sister said so be it. 
When the guy was arrested my niece almost kpaied herself. She rolled and almost rolled under a car. The guy is still at the police custody and her teachers said she has refused to partake in anything in school and hasn't eaten since Monday. Her mom said she's going to take her back home today.

Upon everything that was happening the guy was busy telling her baby calm down, baby I will never leave you. And she was also calling him babe. What has this world turned to?

After researching online, I found MANY users reporting the exact same issue with the new 50MP ultra-wide sensor. Reddit, YouTube, Samsung Community — same problem everywhere.

Because my device was out of warranty, the Dharampeth service centre immediately gave me a ₹4000 quotation instead of acknowledging a possible manufacturing defect.

After endless emails, Samsung support kept repeating: “You have to pay.”

Why should customers pay for Samsung’s hardware failure?

After getting exhausted, I posted on X on 26 April tagging Samsung Electronics India. Only then did they react. Customer Experience Manager Kajal contacted me, and after I shared proof from multiple users online, Samsung finally offered a 73% discount.

I accepted because I was mentally tired of fighting.

On 6 May, I submitted the device. On 7 May, I collected it after paying ₹1000.

Camera fixed?
YES.

New disaster?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF THE VERY NEXT MORNING.

I informed the service centre on WhatsApp. They ignored the messages.

Visited again on 11 May — they “fixed” it.

Two days later?
BACK PANEL AGAIN COMING OFF.

Visited again on 14 May — this time the behavior became shocking.

Instead of accepting poor repair quality, staff started accusing ME of removing the back panel with sharp objects. They checked the device and found ZERO evidence.

Then they saw BGMI installed.

And suddenly their excuse became:
“BGMI is a third-party app. Using third-party apps voids warranty and service.”

Imagine buying one of Samsung’s most powerful flagship phones and being told GAMING can void service support.

When I asked for a written denial letter, they REFUSED.

ONLY after police intervention did the entire attitude of the service centre change. Suddenly:

I followed everything they said.

Result?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF AGAIN.

Since then I have been continuously emailing Samsung support and Kajal from customer experience, asking for a permanent solution or replacement because I cannot travel 13KM repeatedly for the SAME ISSUE.

Today again, after being told to visit the service centre, they AGAIN accused me and AGAIN refused service while refusing to provide any written denial.

The moment I started recording, everyone went silent.

This is the reality of Samsung’s “premium flagship experience” in Nagpur.

Customers are blamed.
Manufacturing defects are ignored.
Poor repairs are repeated.
Written denials are refused.
And consumers are forced into endless visits until they give up.

Absolutely shameful. @SamsungMobile @SamsungIndia

text:
Adventures in El Salvador – Is Bitcoin a Currency

Forward:

Most DKI interns arrive with a clear understanding of macroeconomics and a justified suspicion of the failing fiat system. Even in that exceptional group, Alex Petrou stood apart. He was an early Bitcoiner and his pointed, polite, and reasonable questions of officials from the Bank of England have left them uncomfortable and unable to provide a response. I am pleased to co-author this piece with him. His knowledge of the history of Bitcoin in El Salvador exceeds my own and the section discussing that topic in this white paper reflects his work.

Introduction:

Almost two decades after its creation, there are still debates regarding the true nature of Bitcoin. Some claim it’s not a store of value while admitting that there is nothing on the planet that meets their definition of that term. Others claim it’s a Ponzi scheme, but that makes no sense as a Ponzi scheme relies on using cash collected from later investors to pay early investors. I suspect when people say “Ponzi scheme” they really mean Bitcoin investors are relying on the greater fool theory and expecting deluded future investors to bail them out at ever-higher prices. Many of these people also think bond and equity valuations are sensible despite the fact that those often represent an expansion of the money supply as opposed to real value creation. Some insist that Bitcoin is nothing and backed by nothing while ignoring that fiat currencies have an unbroken multi-thousand-year history of being debased into oblivion. The US dollar is backed by faith and the credit of a government with more than $40 trillion of debt and more than $200 trillion of off-balance sheet liabilities. They think Bitcoin is a fraud while keeping their money in a currency that needs the creation of a quarter of a quadrillion units to meet its obligations.

To me, the most interesting question is whether Bitcoin qualifies as a currency or not. Some claim it’s a commodity based on government regulations. Others advance convoluted and complicated definitions. For the purposes of this article, I’m going to define a currency as something we can use to pay for goods and services directly. The dollar, the yen, and the euro all qualify as currencies. Your grandmother’s fine china doesn’t because it has to be sold and converted into a currency to have usable value. Gold is definitely money, but isn’t a good currency as its value per usable unit is very high and you almost always have to convert it to fiat to use it. Somehow, the measure of a currency in these debates always comes down to “can you use it to buy a coffee”. It’s become a funny cliché, but I also think it’s a meaningful one because it asks the question, “can we use this asset to make a common daily purchase”.

I’m going to relay to you my personal experiences in El Salvador using Bitcoin as a currency. We’ll cover the benefits and drawbacks. I’ll give my opinion on who benefits the most from Bitcoin usage and who pays the highest relative price for it. Finally, I’ll walk you through my experiences with different apps and why I chose one in particular.

text:
Should YOU Use Bitcoin as a Currency:

The answer to whether you should use Bitcoin as a currency depends entirely on where you live and your personal financial circumstances. I’ve seen “Bitcoin accepted here” signs in the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand, Guatemala, and of course, El Salvador. But El Salvador is the only place I’ve seen where Bitcoin is widely accepted. You can use Bitcoin in the US at Burger King and Chipolte, and when buying Miami Dolphin’s tickets. There are places where you can pay your taxes using Bitcoin including Colorado. For most of us, it can be fun to use a Bitcoin app to make a purchase, but you’re going to need traditional banking services in dollars.

Even if you live in El Salvador, the answer still depends on your circumstances. There has been a ton of digital ink spilled over the years regarding the huge fees that banks charge SOME customers. Whether you pay those fees or not depends almost entirely on how much money you have. Many Americans pay to have a checking account, and fees to use an ATM can be enormous. I regularly see ATM fees in the US in the $3 - $5 range, and that can be $8 in foreign countries where you’ll pay an additional huge fee if you make the mistake of accepting the conversion rate offered to you by that foreign bank. I’ve seen fees totaling $15 - $20 on a $100 withdrawal to access “your” money.

Many people pay additional fees to their credit card companies starting with annual charges to have a card. Debit cards deduct funds directly from your checking account and can charge a percentage for that convenience. Both banks and credit card companies charge a wide range of ancillary fees for dealing with overdrafts, sending a wire, or interest for late payments.

Now, let’s take a look at the experience of other people accessing the same banking services and payment networks. For those with greater financial resources, not only is there no fee for a checking account, they will get paid to deposit funds. Accounts of any significant size will receive interest even in a checking account. Annual fees on credit cards are waived as are wire fees for same-day transfers. All ATM fees get refunded including those expensive $8 ones from Guatemala. Credit cards will give customers 1% - 3% cash back on purchases.

Funding a Bitcoin wallet and using it isn’t free. I’ll go through some of those charges in the next section. The point I’m making is whether you’re willing to pay the moderate fees to buy Bitcoin and transfer it to a wallet depends entirely on your situation in the fiat world. If you’re someone who is a source of fees for your bank, then the Bitcoin fees are likely to be small in comparison. For those who are literally paid by their banks and credit card companies to use their services and networks, paying Bitcoin app fees looks like avoidable expense and friction. If you get paid 3% to use your credit card and a Bitcoin app charges you 2%, that’s a 5% difference and a negative incentive. Plus, most Bitcoiners would rather spend continually debased fiat and hodl their Bitcoin as long as possible.

The verdict: Just because Bitcoin can be used as a currency doesn’t mean you’ll want to use it as one.

I want to add one additional important point. If you are willing to spend a few hours learning, you can use Bitcoin to save, invest, pay for things, and to transfer funds almost instantly. You become your own permissionless bank at a time when banks are dangerous. Banks are making a habit of denying services to law-abiding people who express politically incorrect opinions in public. They are denying services to people who engage in the lawful sale of cannabis or firearms. They are making people argue and provide intrusive reasons to access their own cash. I recently received an unpleasant call from Morgan Stanley who wanted to know why I was sending a personal check to a person. The amount was far below the $10,000 reporting requirement. I refused to answer personal questions and my “platinum” service representative warned me that the bank might refuse to send a check which I wanted sent and which I confirmed on the phone call. What happens when “none of your business” becomes insufficient to recover “your” money from a bank?

Some of you might be thinking that you’re not a right-wing politician or commenter and that you don’t buy or sell firearms or cannabis. You might be thinking you have no reason for concern. But the Overton window for “acceptable” opinions and practices shifts wildly, widely, and quickly. Are you sure you’ll always have “acceptable” opinions? Do you want a bank teller or someone in a bank call center to start asking you who you’re sending a check to or to explain to them why you want access to your money? And how sure are you that there won’t be bank bail-ins or nationalizations? Greece did that just last decade.

For those who say bank bail-ins or nationalizations couldn’t happen in the US, it did happen. President Rosevelt made it illegal for US citizens to own gold in 1933 with a penalty of $10,000 and ten years in prison. Once he confiscated everyone’s gold at $20.67 per ounce, he revalued gold to $35.00 per ounce. That means the US government confiscated (stole) 41% of the value of the gold owned by US citizens.

The US government has official debt of $40T plus another $200T of off-balance sheet liabilities like pensions and Social Security. The EU is openly talking about accessing citizen funds on a voluntary basis. No word on what happens when the business recipients chosen by the government fail. Governments in both the US and other countries have previously worked with the banks to access the funds of their citizens. They will again. At the cost of a few hours of educating yourself, you have the ability to use Bitcoin to become your own bank and remove the threat of government control. You don’t have to use Bitcoin as a currency to see there’s a benefit to learning to use it. Alternatively, you could waste hours each year in pointless discussions with Morgan Stanley on whether they want to send the check I instructed them to send. You’re going to spend time dealing with financial issues in the next 12 months. It’s your choice whether that time serves the fiat banking system or allows you to take greater control of your money.

text:
Which Apps to Use:

This section needs to come with an important disclaimer. It reflects my experience and my situation. My plan was to be in El Salvador for 3-4 weeks and I started looking at Bitcoin apps shortly prior to arriving. I also leaned heavily toward apps where I could both buy and use Bitcoin as I didn’t want to recommend a complicated multi-app process for readers. If you were living in El Salvador, or making frequent Bitcoin purchases over a longer time period, your decisions would likely be different and you might consider having multiple apps and multiple wallets. Bitcoin is an open system as opposed to a closed one like Visa or American Express. That means your specific app might not work everywhere. It’s normal for people here to have multiple apps and when one doesn’t work, they quickly transfer sats to a different wallet on a different app and use that one. When it comes to the capabilities of apps I didn’t personally download, I got my information from Grok. I didn’t personally verify it and app capabilities change. Again, I’m relaying my personal experience and this is not intended to be a comprehensive feature comparison for all Bitcoin wallet apps.

Muun, Phoenix, and Blink: I didn’t use these because Grok told me they can only be used to spend Bitcoin. That means you’d have to buy Bitcoin on another platform and transfer it. if you live in El Salvador, it’s worthwhile to absorb the extra friction. As a short-term visitor and as someone who frequently explains Bitcoin to people who are new to the technology, I didn’t want to complicate things with multiple apps and have to transfer sats. I believe that Blink is widely used here and that it provides Bitcoin purchase functionality in some markets. According to Blink’s own website, that functionality is suspended at the time of this writing. These apps are probably good if you have sats in storage and want to transfer them for use (spending). They are not good options if you’re here for a couple of weeks, don’t want to use multiple apps, and aren’t comfortable transferring Bitcoin.

Strike: Like Blink, Strike is widely used in El Salvador. I downloaded the app, quickly set up an account, and verified myself. Then, I went to buy sats and saw that there was a 17-day delay to access my funds. I know banks regularly hold funds for 2-3 days to earn extra interest, but 17 days is abusive. I could have avoided this by paying 2% to use a debit card, but was annoyed by the excessive hold time and didn’t want to give them my business. To their credit, a Strike representative responded to my email quickly and explained that if I made regular purchases, they would reduce the hold time. That might be fine if I were living in El Salvador, but wasn’t an option given that my plan was to spend two weeks at El Zonte (Bitcoin Beach). Again, the apps and options that appeal to you depend on your familiarity with Bitcoin, the amount of time you spend in places where Bitcoin can be used as a currency, and your personal financial situation.

Cash App: This app was recommended to me by Americans who say it’s good for buying and spending Bitcoin. I downloaded the app, set up an account, and got myself verified. This didn’t take a long time to do, but the app has some user interface quirks. Some functionality was in different menus than the main one and due to a misunderstanding, I had to create a second wallet in the same account. It’s not awful, but it’s not easy or intuitive to use. The bigger problem came when I tried to make a Bitcoin purchase.

The app said I needed to verify my email address. I tried to do that four times using two different emails. Nothing worked. I sent a message to customer service and after a few messages, they informed me that I could only initiate a new account and buy Bitcoin from the US. As I was in El Salvador, the app wouldn’t work for either purchases or spending. It was not fooled by setting a VPN to a US server. Customer service suggested trying again when I’m back in the US which won’t happen for another 10 months and would be useless for making Bitcoin purchases in El Salvador. Not a good option!

Coinbase: I have previously used Coinbase to buy Bitcoin, and then transferred those coins to self-custody. In the past, when I transferred funds to Coinbase and purchased Bitcoin, there was a 7-10 day delay to then transfer those coins out of my Coinbase account. I decided to try using my debit card to make a purchase on Coinbase. This would have cost me a small fee, but allowed me to transfer the new sats to a different wallet immediately. You might notice that this violated my “I don’t want to pay fees and I don’t want to use two apps” guidelines, but after wasting a couple of hours setting up accounts and trouble shooting with customer service at Strike and Cash App, I was willing to pay a couple of dollars as fees to be able to relay the experience of using Bitcoin to make purchases.

My newfound flexibility was not rewarded. For Coinbase to allow me to use my debit card, they had to send 1-2 tiny transactions to test the account. They didn’t do that. I deleted the debit card and re-entered everything. Still no test transaction. I called customer service and got a representative in India who told me to delete the debit card and then try again. He had difficulty understanding that I had done this multiple times. I did it again with him on the phone with the same lack of success. He told me I had to call my bank. I informed him that the bank had access to the same information I had and that calling them was a waste of time. He insisted that was the next step.

I called my bank and they told me what I already knew: There was no tiny transaction from Coinbase. I called customer service again, and got a woman from The Philippines. I told her everything that had happened. She asked me to try deleting the debit card and re-entering it. She then suggested calling my bank. I’m 100% certain that neither of these “customer service” representatives were listening to me and don’t care if they help me solve a problem or not. They just follow a script. Finally, she told me to wait for 24 hours and if there was no transaction, I could try re-entering everything again. So, the plan from Coinbase was to wait 24 hours and then do the same things that didn’t work the previous day. It’s 3 weeks later and I still haven’t seen the Coinbase micro-transaction.

@River: This app was the clear winner. I downloaded River, set up an account, and verified myself with photos of my identification and a live selfie in 12 minutes. I clicked “buy Bitcoin” and bought enough to buy dinner. The transaction was instant and cost me 1.25% including the bid/offer spread. The user interface was by far the best I’ve seen. The one downside was it took a week for my purchased Bitcoin to become usable. Using the app was incredibly easy; click “send”, click “scan a QR”, scan the code, enter the amount you want to spend. The merchant sees the transfer instantly. It’s faster and easier than using a credit card and allows you to enter the amount rather than the merchant. River was the one app with the functionality to buy and spend Bitcoin, with a hold time below 17 days, that actually worked. It had the lowest fees and the best user interface.

Disclosure: River sponsors DKI. My partner code with them is https://t.co/YcZ8RAPmfO. You might draw the conclusion that I’m biased. When I downloaded the app, set up my account, and purchased Bitcoin, I did that on my own. River did not know who was setting up the account or purchasing Bitcoin, and I did so without any assistance, special treatment, or reduced fees. I have relayed my personal experience with each app accurately. Your experience may vary from mine.

text:
Illegal Infiltration & Fake Documentation:-A Real Case I Handled

Home Minister @AmitShah ji has held that the population of Muslims in India has increased due to illegal infiltration. Let me share a real case I personally handled about 5–6 years ago in Mumbai, one among many that reveal how deep this problem runs. Please do read to understand the rot.

1. The Client’s Request:- One evening after court hours, a Muslim gentleman known to me came to my office. He had given his premises in Govandi, Mumbai, on a leave and license agreement to a family of 6/7 people.
Even after the agreement expired, the family refused to vacate.

I perused his papers and assured him of appropriate legal action. He then asked if the matter could be resolved sooner than usual.
When I explained that such cases typically take little time, he hesitated and what he said next stunned me.

2. The Shocking Revelation :- He quietly said, “Sir, those tenants are not Indians, they are Bangladeshis.”

That single sentence changed everything. Two thoughts struck me instantly:
1. Why hadn’t he mentioned this earlier?
2. How did they even get valid Aadhaar and PAN cards as visible in the agreement?

3. The Investigation:- On examining the documents, everything looked perfectly legitimate; Aadhaar, PAN, ration card, even voter ID.
We filed RTIs, involved the local police, and began to dig deeper.

Gradually, the truth surfaced, the birth certificate forming the basis of all these documents was forged.

Using that single forged certificate from 1967, the accused had created a full legal identity for himself and his family, including Aadhaar, PAN, ration card, and voter ID.

4. A Web of Fraud:- It didn’t stop there. The man had used the same method to obtain documents for his wife and children. His son was even married to an Indian Muslim woman, effectively merging into the Indian population.

During the investigation, we uncovered an organized network, a full-fledged industry operating to regularize illegal immigrants by manufacturing fake Indian identities that pass every verification test.

5. The Larger Problem:-India’s diversity makes such infiltration even easier. People entering from Bangladesh, Pakistan, Myanmar, or Nepal often resemble locals making visual identification almost impossible.

Add to this the corruption that exists from border checkpoints to administrative offices, and you have a perfect ecosystem for illegal population growth.

In this very case, we found the involvement of certain officials, and shockingly, even a few lawyers.

6. A Moment That Exposed the Rot:- One of those lawyers, representing the Bangladeshi accused, told my Muslim junior,
“How can you do this? This is a matter of religion.”
My junior stood firm and warned him of a complaint before the Bar Council.

This single moment revealed how some individuals, blinded by religious or political motives, are actively protecting those who illegally enter and settle in India.

7. The Unanswered Question:- 
This wasn’t the only case, I have come across several similar ones.
Despite being aware of this menace for years, successive governments have failed to implement a robust national mechanism to identify and deport such individuals.

8. The Hope:- Now that the Home Minister himself has spoken openly about the issue, one can only hope it translates into real, concrete action. India needs a firm, technology-backed, corruption-proof mechanism to detect and remove non-Indians living here on forged documents.

Illegal infiltration is not just a demographic concern, it’s a threat to national integrity, law, and fairness. The time for acknowledgment is over.
The time for action has arrived.

@AmitShahOffice

text:
Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

In 2023, I  reported from #Manipur regarding  #pellet gun injuries suffered by 17 yr old Kishan Loitongbam. text:
"They could have killed my son": Mother demands answers

A Montreal man was pepper-sprayed, kicked, dragged across the pavement,  and stabbed by a group of masked men near Place-des-Arts, an attack that  left him with a punctured and collapsed lung, broken ribs and severe  facial fractures.

A 24-year-old man is speaking out after a brutal attack by more  than ten men of colour near Place-des-Arts metro station in downtown  Montreal left him hospitalized with serious injuries.

For security reasons and out of fear of retaliation, Rebel News is protecting the identities of both the victim and his mother.

Montreal police confirmed that a robbery involving multiple  suspects occurred on August 26. According to police, the victim was  pepper-sprayed, beaten and stabbed with a sharp object.

The victim told Rebel News he had been with friends near the  metro when a group of roughly two dozen masked individuals appeared  nearby. He described them as dressed mostly in black and said, “They  were all wearing COVID masks to hide their faces.”

Later that night, he says the group approached him from behind.

“One of them put his hand on my shoulder. He pulled me around, and immediately I… I got hit in the face with pepper spray.”

What followed, according to the victim, was a prolonged and vicious beating.

“Then they started punching me, kicking me, and dragging me  along the ground by my bag,” he said. “During that, I was stabbed  several times in the chest area, in the back.”

One stab wound punctured his lung. “Air was going in and out through my back. And I didn’t even know I’d been stabbed.”

He says his lung later collapsed and doctors had to remove both  air and blood before reinflating it. He also reported broken ribs,  facial fractures and continuing problems with vision in his left eye.

His approximately $5,000 Louis Vuitton bag, phone, cards and keys were stolen. Perhaps most disturbing to the family is what allegedly happened around them.

“It affects me quite a bit,” the victim said after being asked  about bystanders and friends who did not intervene. “I would at least  have intervened.”

His mother remains shaken. “Oh my God! I was angry, I was devastated, and I was worried,” she said after seeing video of the attack.

Asked about safety in Montreal, her answer was unequivocal: “There is no safety in Montreal anymore.”

Police have told Rebel News that no arrests have been made so far.

On August 28, 2026, two patients who had come to Savanur Taluk Hospital in Haveri district, Karnataka, for treatment were allegedly made to manually remove human waste from an overflowing sewage/cesspit on the hospital premises.

According to police and media reports, the patients were allegedly asked to inspect the overflowing sewage and subsequently began clearing the waste using buckets provided by the hospital. Police said they were allegedly offered better medical treatment and medicines in exchange for doing the work.  

The incident came to light after nearby residents noticed the activity and intervened. Photographs and videos of the patients cleaning the pit subsequently circulated widely. The pit was later cleaned using municipal machinery.  

The hospital’s administrative medical officer, Dr. Shankar Y. Hiregowdar, and senior nursing officer Vanitha Kurundawad were suspended by Karnataka’s Health and Family Welfare Services Department pending a departmental inquiry. According to the government order reported by India Today and PTI, the nurse was alleged to have instructed patients known to her and their relatives to manually clean the hospital cesspit, while Dr. Hiregowdar was held responsible for allowing the incident to take place.  

A police case was also registered at Savanur Police Station. Reports state that the case invokes Section 125 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita along with provisions of the Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act, 2013, which prohibits the employment of people for manual removal of human excreta.  

There was also a prior warning about the sanitation problem. According to police, the cesspit had begun overflowing and Dr. Hiregowdar had written to municipal authorities on August 27, a day before the reported incident, requesting assistance. Police said no response had been received before the patients were allegedly made to undertake the cleaning.  

The departmental inquiry is intended to establish the circumstances and responsibility for what happened. The allegations should therefore be distinguished from findings that may emerge from the investigation.

No patient should have to perform hazardous sanitation work in order to receive medical care. Human dignity cannot be conditional on access to treatment.

Sources: The Indian Express, India Today, Hindustan Times, PTI/Deccan Chronicle, Salar News.

AP Police impersonated the FBI

Subject: Request for Investigation - Andhra Pradesh Police Officer Identified “FBI” as Requesting Organization in X/Twitter Law-Enforcement Request Concerning a U.S. Citizen

To:
Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
The Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3)
@FBI @FBIDirectorKash @FBITampa @TheJusticeDept  
U.S. Department of Justice

Dear Director / Appropriate Federal Officials:

I am a United States citizen residing in the United States. I respectfully submit this complaint and request for review concerning an apparent misrepresentation of U.S. federal law-enforcement identity in connection with a social-media investigation initiated by the Andhra Pradesh Police in India.

I. Summary of the complaint

I recently received a notification from X Support concerning a law-enforcement request submitted to X regarding my X account.
The X communication initially stated that the request had been submitted by the “FBI.”

However, X subsequently provided an important correction. X expressly stated:

“However, this request did not come from the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)”

X further stated that the request actually came from the Andhra Pradesh Police and identified the submitting individual as:

Name: A V Bramham
Position: Inspector of Police
Organization entered by requester: FBI
Email: guntururbansp-ap@gov.in
Location: Guntur, Andhra Pradesh, India
Country: India

X further stated:
“it is unclear why the Andhra Pradesh Police wrote ‘FBI’ as the sender organization.”
I have preserved the X communication and can provide the original notification and screenshot as evidence.
II. Why I am requesting U.S. government review
I fully recognize that foreign law-enforcement agencies may communicate with U.S. companies through legitimate international law-enforcement cooperation channels.
The issue here is different.

According to X’s own records, an Andhra Pradesh Police official submitted the request, but the requesting organization was entered as “FBI.”

I therefore respectfully request that the appropriate U.S. authorities determine:

Whether the FBI had any involvement whatsoever in this request to X.

Whether any FBI office, agent, liaison officer, or other U.S. government agency authorized, participated in, or communicated with Andhra Pradesh Police concerning my X account.
Whether the Andhra Pradesh Police official knowingly or inadvertently represented himself or his agency as the FBI when submitting the request to X.

Whether the use of “FBI” as the requesting organization was intended to obtain greater credibility, priority, cooperation, disclosure, restriction, or removal of content from X.

Whether X received any other law-enforcement request from Andhra Pradesh Police concerning my account in which the FBI was similarly identified.

Whether this conduct implicates any U.S. federal criminal, civil-rights, cyber, impersonation, transnational-repression, or other federal jurisdiction.

Whether the conduct should be referred to another appropriate federal authority for investigation.
III. First Amendment / transnational-repression concern
The underlying matter concerns social-media content posted on X and alleged violations of Indian law.
I am particularly concerned because I am a U.S. citizen residing in the United States, and the governmental action concerns my online speech and political commentary.
I understand that the United States cannot simply disregard legitimate foreign criminal investigations. However, I am requesting that U.S. authorities determine whether a foreign law-enforcement agency has attempted to use the identity or authority of a U.S. federal agency to influence or restrict constitutionally protected activity occurring in the United States.
The FBI itself recognizes transnational repression as an issue that may affect people in the United States and specifically directs individuals who believe they have been affected by transnational repression to report the matter to the FBI.
IV. Request for preservation and investigation of evidence
I respectfully request that the appropriate agency consider preserving and/or obtaining, where legally appropriate:
the original law-enforcement request submitted by Andhra Pradesh Police to X;

all metadata associated with that request;

the identity and authentication information associated with the requester;

the date and time of submission;

all representations made by the requester concerning his identity and governmental organization;
any attachments, legal documents, FIRs, court orders, or other materials submitted to X;

any subsequent communications between X and Andhra Pradesh Police concerning my account;
any communications between U.S. government agencies and Andhra Pradesh Police concerning this matter; and
any evidence showing whether “FBI” was entered intentionally or accidentally.
V. Request for clarification from the FBI
I respectfully request confirmation of the following:
Did the FBI have any involvement in, authorization of, or knowledge of this particular request to X?
If the answer is no, I respectfully request that the FBI consider whether the circumstances warrant investigation or referral concerning the apparent use of the FBI’s identity by a foreign law-enforcement official.
VI. Good-faith submission
I am not asking the U.S. government to interfere with a legitimate Indian criminal investigation.
My request is narrower:
I am asking the United States government to determine whether an Indian police official represented himself or his agency as the FBI when submitting a law-enforcement request concerning a U.S. citizen’s social-media account, and whether that conduct violated any U.S. law or raised a transnational-repression or foreign-government intimidation concern.

I am prepared to provide the original X communication, screenshots, account information, relevant posts, and any notices received from Andhra Pradesh Police.

I respectfully request that this complaint be logged, reviewed, and referred to the appropriate federal authority if the receiving office does not have jurisdiction.

Thank you for your attention to this matter.
Respectfully,

U.S. Citizen

text:
The Pothole Is Not an Accident

On the morning of Saturday, 13 June 2026, a woman named Kantha was riding her two-wheeler along the Siddapur road near Marathahalli, dropping her daughter Neha at college. It had rained heavily the night before, and the potholes had filled with water, which is the detail that makes them invisible. She hit one, lost control and fell. A school bus coming from behind ran her over. She died on the road, in front of her daughter.

A case was registered at the Whitefield traffic police station. Against the bus.

That is the whole architecture of the problem in one line. There is always a vehicle to charge. There is never a road to charge.

Kantha's death was not a freak event. In Bengaluru it is closer to a season. The National Crime Records Bureau counts deaths caused by the negligence of civic bodies, meaning bad roads, potholes, open drains, collapsing infrastructure, electrocution. Bengaluru has ranked first among Indian metros in that category for six consecutive years. Delhi, bigger and denser and not famous for good roads, recorded four in a year when Bengaluru recorded seventeen. Either Bengaluru's roads are uniquely lethal, or every other city is better at not counting.

The national picture, in passing: figures tabled in Parliament record 9,438 people killed in pothole crashes between 2020 and 2024, about five a day, the toll rising 53% across those years. The Supreme Court called such numbers frightening as far back as 2018. Yet the same table shows Andhra Pradesh, Bihar and Goa reporting zero pothole deaths in five years. Not zero potholes. Zero deaths. That is not a measurement. It is a filing decision.

A pothole death exists, legally, only if a police officer writes the word pothole into an FIR. Most do not. The crash becomes rash driving, or a hit-and-run. There is a driver to arrest and a section of the penal code that fits him. There is no section that fits an engineer who certified a road that dissolved in the first monsoon.

Bengaluru has a case that shows exactly how that works. On 6 February 2021, Tasdeeq Bushra, nineteen and in her first year of MBBS, was riding home along Hennur Main Road. She swerved to avoid a pothole. A truck hit her scooter from behind, she fell, and she went under the wheels.

The truck belonged to the Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike. The city's own civic body owned the vehicle that killed her, and the road, and the pothole she was avoiding. The driver was arrested under Section 304A, causing death by negligence. The agency was not. Her father, Mushtaq Ahmed, put it better than any court has: "We have lost our only child. Whom will we pin the blame on? The vehicle was BBMP's and so was the driver, the roads were poorly built by them." BBMP, the water board and the electricity utility then blamed one another, which is the standard procedure.

Two details from what followed are worth sitting with. The FIR did not mention the pothole. And the pothole was filled within hours of her death. The evidence was repaired faster than the case was built.

Hers is not an outlier, it is the template. The News Minute traced thirteen pothole deaths in Bengaluru between 2017 and 2022. Families compensated: zero. Officials held accountable: zero. Not for want of a policy. BBMP had notified one, three lakh rupees for a death, and reporters found zonal chief engineers who did not know it existed and had never received a claim. A right nobody is told about is not a right, it is a press release. When Ashwin, twenty-seven, died on a pothole in MS Palya, police first blamed him for riding irresponsibly. His mother fought to get one line into the FIR naming unnamed civic officers. Nothing came of it.

The courts have been trying for a decade. A petition filed in 2015 is still running, and the High Court has reprimanded the corporation repeatedly, once issuing a contempt notice after BBMP resisted paying compensation at all. At one hearing, BBMP informed the court that Bengaluru contained 221 potholes in total. The court told it to be honest.

Then came the deadline. After a student named Dhanushree was crushed by a tipper lorry in September 2025 while swerving around a pothole, the Chief Minister announced that Bengaluru would be pothole-free by the end of October, with eleven hundred crore rupees sanctioned. Officials counted potholes by the thousand and announced them filled. The deadline was missed and replaced with another. In Whitefield, residents watched gravel tipped into holes, gravel that scatters as soon as vehicles pass over it.

Here is how that pothole-free year ended. On 20 November, three weeks after the deadline, Shantamma, forty-six, riding pillion home from work, fell on a broken stretch in Hulimavu and was run over by a truck. Police blamed potholes and loose gravel. On 17 December, Tabrez, thirty-two, swerved near Nelamangala and put his front wheel into an unbarricaded pipeline pit. He died at NIMHANS two days later. Not a pothole, strictly. The same disease.

Then the rains came back in June, and so did the holes, and so did Kantha's funeral.

The exhausting part is that the effort is real. The money is spent, the holes are counted and announced, and they return on schedule, because filling a pothole is not building a road. A pothole is the visible end of a chain: a specification diluted, a layer skipped, a bill cleared, an inspection signed. Every hole in a Bengaluru road has a name attached to it somewhere. None of those names ever reaches an FIR.

A drunk driver goes to jail. A negligent engineer gets transferred. A contractor whose road failed in ten weeks bids for the next tender. The person who dies becomes a line in a table.

Bengaluru has led that table for six years and has still not produced one official who lost a job over a death. Until a road failure is something a person can be charged with, the ritual continues: a monsoon, a hole, a two-wheeler, a bus behind it, a case against the driver, gravel by the weekend, and a family being told that what happened to them was an accident.

It was not an accident. Someone built that.

text:
IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.
